findings.note: Flipping the right pair (dusk:spring to spring:dusk) yields the same start-of-cycle : end-of-cycle relation as dawn:winter, so a player could solve this ordering and be wrongly marked incorrect. Both halves read as: "start of one cycle paired with end of another (day-start : year-end)" and "flipped to spring:dusk, start of one cycle paired with end of another (year-start : day-end)".

notes:
Fix set-time-span: spring/winter is not a true opposite-pole pair like dawn/dusk, allowing a flipped cross-reading (spring:dusk) to satisfy the same start/end-of-cycle relation, creating an accidental alternate solution.
- set-time-span: Spring and winter are adjacent, not opposite, seasons, so flipping the right pair (dusk:spring) reads as the same start/end-of-cycle relation as dawn:winter, giving a valid alternate solution.
  Try: Replace 'winter' with 'autumn' (or 'fall') so the pair is spring:autumn, true opposite poles of the year matching dawn:dusk
  Or: Replace both season words with 'summer' and 'winter' (solstice opposites) instead of spring/winter
  Or: Keep spring/winter but change 'dawn'/'dusk' to a pair with less symmetric flip potential, e.g. 'sunrise'/'sunset' plus verify no flip reading remains
Do not change: set-plant-kind, set-worked-tool, set-bee-lack — no allowlisted finding touches them.

persisted.note: A player can read this as a consistent 'beginning of cycle : beginning of cycle' paired with 'closing phase : closing phase', since autumn is commonly treated as the year's waning phase just as dusk is the day's waning phase. Both halves read as: "dawn and spring are both the beginning phase of their respective cycle" and "dusk and autumn are both the closing/declining phase of their respective cycle".

Both halves consistently pair opposite phases of their cycles (start-vs-decline and end-vs-start), which a player could read as a deliberate 'inverse phase' relation mirroring the intended opposite-poles idea. Both halves read as: "dawn (start of day) paired against autumn (decline of year) — opposite-phase pairing" and "dusk (end of day) paired against spring (start of year) — opposite-phase pairing".
